outcome: Redington turns the Linux estate into a managed, auditable population with patch state that can be reported rather than reconstructed.
overview: A Linux estate grows one server at a time and nobody decides to standardise it — versions spread, patching is done by whoever built the box, and the first honest inventory usually arrives during an audit. Red Hat Enterprise Linux with Satellite makes the estate a managed population instead of a collection: one supported operating system, one content view controlling which packages a host may receive, and patch state that can be reported rather than reconstructed. The gain is auditability and a shorter path from a published vulnerability to a patched fleet. Redington measures patch latency and the unmanaged host count against what discovery actually found.

benefits.text: Patch state across the Linux estate becomes reportable rather than reconstructed
benefits.limits: Only covers hosts registered to the management server; anything nobody enrols stays invisible, which is why the unmanaged count is measured separately

benefits.text: A supported operating system with a published lifecycle replaces version drift
benefits.limits: Subscription-model claim: the benefit depends on the customer consolidating onto the subscription rather than running it alongside what it was meant to replace

benefits.text: Build time for a new server drops because the base image and its content are defined once
benefits.limits: Applies to new builds; existing hosts still have to be brought onto the standard, and that is migration work with its own cost

residency: Management server and content mirror run inside the customer estate; no host inventory or package data needs to leave it

notFor.situation: An estate already standardised on another commercially supported Linux
notFor.why: Two supported distributions means two patch cadences, two content pipelines and two support contracts for one job

notFor.situation: A fleet that is mostly ephemeral cloud instances rebuilt from images
notFor.why: Long-lived host patching is the problem this solves; an immutable fleet solves it by rebuilding

scope:
Model: Redington solutions engineering with an accredited Red Hat implementation partner · Duration: 6–10 weeks to a reporting fleet, depending on host count and change-window availability
Support model: Vendor subscription support for the operating system and management server; Redington coordinates the vendor case. Optional managed patch operations against an agreed cycle.
1) Discovery — full host inventory including unmanaged hosts, version and patch-state baseline
2) Design — base image, content-view model, environment promotion path and exception process
3) Build — Satellite deployment, content mirroring, views and reporting
4) Enrol and hand over — phased registration by environment, first patch wave, runbook handover
deliverables: Patch state for every enrolled host is produced from the reporting layer without manual assembly
A new host built from the standard image registers and receives its environment content unaided
The customer team promotes a content view between two environments without assistance
